title: Drew Streib - Servers and NAO
speaker: Drew Streib
summary: Drew Streib, operator of the public NetHack server nethack.alt.org (NAO) and author of dgamelaunch, describes the history of public roguelike servers and why players use them: shared bones, verified games, standardized versions, play from work and community. He explains dgamelaunch and ttyrec-based live game watching, which accelerated how quickly players learn to ascend, plus the server's architecture, security challenges, crash reporting to the DevTeam, the move to AWS and a websocket browser terminal. He covers server statistics and what makes a game impressive, the large ttyrec archive's use for analytics and bots, hosting the NetHack wiki, and a call to broaden accessibility to grow the community.

insights.claim: Early roguelike multiplayer features like shared bones files and in-game mail came from university shell servers, and early public NetHack servers were mostly in Finland and northern Europe.
insights.detail: Streib recalls fishpool in Finland had only 22 ascensions listed in January 2001. He started NAO in 2001 because there were no servers with local latency for him.
insights.quote: the servers were actually local servers you would shell into um and the bones files shared games

insights.claim: Public servers make bones files from other players a real part of NetHack, since a solo local player rarely encounters them.
insights.detail: Streib says stumbling randomly on someone's bones, perhaps a wizard's, was his only realistic chance to ascend, and felt less like cheating than deliberately inserting a level.
insights.quote: i had no opportunity to see bones as a user that wasn't at the time at a university on a server with other people playing

insights.claim: Verified server games give scores meaning, so NAO takes a hard line against restoring games or save-scumming, though Streib warns fewer people care about bragging rights than you think.
insights.detail: Streib's main reason for running a server was proving his achievements; he lost interest in Diablo when its online verification broke. Later he says NAO refuses restores so a score sitting there 'actually means something'.
insights.quote: i promise you fewer people care about your bragging rights on these verified games and you think they do

insights.claim: Live game watching on public servers doesn't change NetHack but greatly accelerates the learning curve, so players who once took years to ascend now often ascend within weeks.
insights.detail: Players at first pushed back because they didn't want their secrets given away, so NAO displays a banner saying all games are watched. Streib calls ttyrec watching a 'prehistoric Twitch'.
insights.quote: it doesn't change the game it just accelerates the learning curve

insights.claim: dgamelaunch is a generic front end for any TTY game that forks a ttyrec spooling process for watching alongside the game, with in-game mail as the only player interaction.
insights.detail: Streib repurposed ttyrec, which someone else made for a different purpose, and uses simple mail to message players mid-game. It now fronts many games, mostly NetHack variants; website and IRC bots run outside the jail.
insights.quote: this is basically the front end i built it for nethack it really is for any tty based front end

insights.claim: Running roguelikes on a public server is a security headache: game binaries have bugs and options editors must be locked down so they can't write arbitrary files.
insights.detail: Streib advises separating a game server from other services because it has 'enough holes to drive trucks through', backing up often and getting a co-admin. He credits co-admin Pasi Kallinen (paxed) with carrying NAO for years.
insights.quote: an amazing amount of time goes into editing and options that are there to remove its ability to write random files across the disk

insights.claim: A busy public server surfaces rare bugs that individual players never hit, making it a useful source of core dumps for the NetHack DevTeam.
insights.detail: With thousands of games a month, a one-in-a-thousand bug shows up on the server even if not for others.
insights.quote: we we have been able to be a good feed basically for for core dumps and such

insights.claim: NAO stays on simple Linux instances rather than containers or serverless because live watching needs fast open sockets and Streib avoids patching stock game binaries.
insights.detail: Modified binaries could save to object storage on transient instances, but these are long-running games kept as stock as possible. Moving to AWS got NAO out of the hardware failure business.
insights.quote: live game watching has kind of been the big one the main feature that everyone seems to like

insights.claim: A JavaScript terminal over websockets (Chromium's hterm) lets players run NetHack in a browser, including through networks that block telnet.
insights.detail: Streib presents it as reaching people who previously couldn't telnet in, such as at work, through TLS interception that supports websocket pass-through.
insights.quote: there's a javascript implemented terminal if you haven't tried it yet at work and you previously couldn't telnet in give it a try

insights.claim: In NetHack, high score tracks improvement only before a player ascends; for serial ascenders, low-turn, low-score and high-conduct ascensions are the more impressive feats.
insights.detail: Streib says he focused on high scores early, but lower-score ascensions usually mean a better player who didn't need to stockpile preparation. He'd like more stats on conducts.
insights.quote: low turn games low scoring games are actually more impressive and high conduct games than our high scorers

insights.claim: NAO's roughly 200 GB of ttyrec recordings capture every situation and what worked, and have been used for analytics and bots, one of which ascended on a public server.
insights.detail: The bot used mechanics like pudding farming that are nerfed in NetHack 3.6, and no bot had yet beaten 3.6. Streib offers the archive to anyone who ships him a hard drive.
insights.quote: there has been one bot ascension on a public server on nao in the past

insights.claim: Being spoiled doesn't ruin NetHack: knowing what will happen doesn't save you when you make the wrong choice, and many fully spoiled players still can't win.
insights.detail: Streib contrasts the old effort of browsing scattered spoiler pages with the modern NetHack wiki, which he co-hosts and plans to move to a non-profit so it outlives him and stays ad-free.
insights.quote: just knowing what's going to happen doesn't save you when you make the wrong choice

insights.claim: Keeping a roguelike community alive requires broadening access, for example browser and phone play, rather than dismissing low-barrier newcomers.
insights.detail: Streib admits he once rolled his eyes at the Reddit NetHack crowd but now sees them as important. His call to action is that accessibility to a big audience fills the pipeline of new players, alongside offering more game choice on servers.
insights.quote: accessibility to a big audience is a big deal and anything that we can do to kind of broaden that

insights.claim: Server game watching enabled live mentoring: an IRC helper could watch a stuck player's game and tell them exactly what to do.
insights.detail: An audience member (an event organizer) described ascending on NAO with a friend sending in-game mail advice and IRC helpers watching her game. Streib calls this a more advanced spoiler and is fine with it.
insights.quote: what's your name on nethack.org i'll go watch the game and see like like oh open your inventory
